'''''Aglaonema''''' is a [[genus]] of [[flowering plant]]s in the arum family, [[Araceae]]. They are native to [[tropics|tropical]] and [[subtropics|subtropical]] regions of [[Asia]] and [[New Guinea]].<ref name=i>[https://apps.kew.org/wcsp/namedetail.do?name_id=4599 Kew World Checklist of Selected Plant Families]</ref><ref name=china>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=100818 ''Aglaonema''.] Flora of China.</ref> They are known commonly as '''Chinese evergreens'''.<ref name=chen>Chen, J., et al. [https://edis.ifas.ufl.edu/ep160 Cultural Guidelines for Commercial Production of Interiorscape ''Aglaonema''.] ENH957. Environmental Horticulture. Florida Cooperative Extension Service. University of Florida IFAS. 2003.</ref>

==Description==
These are [[evergreen]] [[perennial plant|perennial]]s with stems growing erect or decumbent and creeping. Stems that grow along the ground may root at the nodes. There is generally a crown of wide leaf blades which in wild species are often [[Variegation|variegated]] with silver and green coloration. The [[inflorescence]] bears unisexual flowers in a [[spadix (botany)|spadix]], with a short zone of female flowers near the base and a wider zone of male flowers nearer the tip. The fruit is a fleshy [[berry (botany)|berry]] that ripens red. The fruit is a thin layer covering one large seed.<ref name=china/>

Plants of the genus are native to humid, shady [[Tropical and subtropical moist broadleaf forests|tropical forest]] habitat.<ref name=chen/>

==Cultivation and uses==
[[File:Aglaonema costatum 003.JPG|thumb|right|200px|''[[Aglaonema costatum]]'']]
''Aglaonema'' have been grown as [[luck]]-bringing [[ornamental plant]]s in Asia for centuries.<ref name=chen/> They were introduced to [[Western world|the West]] in 1885,<ref name=chen/> when they were first brought to the [[Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew]].<ref>Chen, J., et al. (2004). [https://web.archive.org/web/20120124025005/http://aob.oxfordjournals.org/content/93/2/157.full Genetic relationships of ''Aglaonema'' species and cultivars inferred from AFLP markers.] ''Annals of Botany'' 93(2), 157-66.</ref> They have been cultivated, [[hybrid (biology)|hybridized]], and bred into a wide array of [[cultivar]]s. They live in low-light conditions and are popular [[houseplant]]s.<ref name=chen/>

This mainly tropical genus is known for its intolerance of cold temperatures. Chilling injury can begin at {{convert|15|C|F}}.<ref name=chill>Chen, J., et al. [https://edis.ifas.ufl.edu/ep103 Chilling Injury in Tropical Foliage Plants: II. ''Aglaonema''.] ENH843. Environmental Horticulture. Florida Cooperative Extension Service. University of Florida IFAS. 2001.</ref> The injury manifests in dark, greasy-looking patches on the foliage.<ref name=chill/>

Cultivars have been selected for their shape and size, and especially for the color and pattern of the leaves. Many have white or cream-colored stems. Some have also been developed to tolerate colder temperatures.<ref name=chen/> The most common cultivar is 'Silver Queen',<ref name=chen/> which has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/92017/Aglaonema-Silver-Queen/Details |title=RHS Plant Selector ''Aglaonema'' 'Silver Queen' AGM / RHS Gardening |publisher=Apps.rhs.org.uk |date= |access-date=2020-03-12}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = November 2018 | page = 4 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | website = www.rhs.org | access-date = 27 February 2020}}</ref>

Most [[plant propagation|propagation]] of ''Aglaonema'' is done with cuttings and by dividing the [[Basal shoot|basal shoots]]. Care of the houseplant involves protecting it from cold temperatures and excessive sunlight and removing any [[Inflorescence|inflorescences]] that develop, which can prolong the life of the plant. It requires moist soil, and while some cultivars require a small amount of [[fertilizer]], plants are easily injured when oversupplemented.<ref name=chen/> ''Aglaonema'' are prone to false mites (''[[Brevipalpus]] californicus''). They may also acquire populations of [[nematode]]s, such as [[root-knot nematode]]s and ''[[Pratylenchus]]'' species, which cause root lesions.<ref>Conover, C. A., et al. [http://mrec.ifas.ufl.edu/FoliageDigest/v4n8.html ''Aglaonema'' Production Guide for Commercial Growers.] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130621124740/http://mrec.ifas.ufl.edu/FoliageDigest/v4n8.html |date=June 21, 2013 }} Foliage Digest. Mid-Florida Research & Education Center. University of Florida IFAS.</ref> [[Plant pathogen|Pathogens]] include the [[fungus]] ''[[Myrothecium roridum]]'' and [[bacteria]] such as ''[[Pseudomonas cichorii]]'', ''[[Erwinia chrysanthemi]]'', and ''[[Xanthomonas campestris]]'', which can all cause [[leaf spot]]. ''[[Colletotrichum]]'' fungi can cause [[canker|anthracnose]].<ref>Moorman, G. W. [http://extension.psu.edu/pests/plant-diseases/all-fact-sheets/aglaonema-diseases ''Aglaonema'' Diseases.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170820123345/http://extension.psu.edu/pests/plant-diseases/all-fact-sheets/aglaonema-diseases |date=2017-08-20 }} Penn State Extension. The Pennsylvania State University. 2013.</ref>

The [[NASA Clean Air Study]] determined that the species ''modestum'' of this plant genus was effective at removing common household air toxins [[formaldehyde]] and [[benzene]].

''Aglaonema'' plants are [[poisonous]] due to [[calcium oxalate]] crystals. If ingested they cause irritation of the mucous membranes, and the juice can cause skin irritation and painful [[rash]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Toxic Plants (by common name) |url=http://ucanr.edu/sites/poisonous_safe_plants/Toxic_Plants_by_common_Name_659 |publisher=[[University of California]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221007131304/http://ucanr.edu/sites/poisonous_safe_plants/Toxic_Plants_by_common_Name_659/ |archive-date=7 October 2022}}</ref>
